chunks: DCM vs CCM in a buck converter. The question: What is the difference between discontinuous and continuous operation?
The difference is whether the inductor current ever falls to zero. In CCM it never does, so the current just goes up and down.
In DCM it falls to zero partway through the cycle and stays there until the next one starts. Which mode you are in depends on the load.
Picture traffic on a road. In CCM, cars are always moving past a point; the flow rises and falls but never stops.
In DCM, the flow dies down to nothing between waves of cars, so the road sits empty for a while.
A lighter load is like less traffic overall, and below a certain point the road empties out each cycle.
The analogy is loose: in a buck the "empty" time ends only because the next switch-on starts it.
To the right of K crit (heavy load, CCM) the curves are flat: M equals D regardless of load. To the left (light load, DCM) M climbs above D .
Left unregulated, at no load M to 1 : the output floats up to V in . This is why a DCM converter needs the controller to cut the duty cycle as the load falls.
CCM: continuous conduction mode, where the inductor current stays above zero. DCM: discontinuous conduction mode, where it reaches zero and stays there for part of the cycle.
Ripple current ( change in I L ): the peak-to-peak swing of the inductor current ("What sets the inductor current slope").
Boundary: the load where the valley of the ripple just touches zero, I out equals change in I L over 2 .
Diode emulation: switching the bottom switch off at zero current so no current flows backward.
Let the ripple current be 1 amps peak-to-peak. At a 2 amps load the current swings from 1. 5 amps to 2. 5 amps and never touches zero: CCM. At a 0.
5 amps load it swings from 0 amps to 1 amps, exactly on the boundary I out equals change in I L over 2 . Below 0. 5 amps it spends part of each cycle at zero: DCM.
That is the whole idea.
"In CCM the inductor current never reaches zero; in DCM it falls to zero and rests for part of the cycle, so there are three switching states instead of two.
The boundary is at I out equals change in I L over 2 .
In CCM the output is D V in regardless of load; in DCM the gain depends on the load, so the duty cycle must shrink as the load drops.
DCM also has higher peak current, ringing at the idle interval, and a more first-order loop response, but better light-load efficiency."
